excerpt: LLMs and the illusion of competence One thing that I worry about with coding in the age of AI is that the uncritical use of LLMs can make us believe we are far more competent than we really are. In general, the more expert you become in your field, the better you can judge what someone (or an LLM) says about it, and conversely, the less you know in a field, the less likely you are to question what people say about it1. This happens to all of us, sometimes in comical ways: while reading a newspaper, you may come across an article about some technical topic you already know really well. Reading the article, you’ll likely notice things that are off, oversimplified, dubious. You’ll think “this journalist doesn’t know what they’re talking about”. And then you’ll turn the page and continue reading the rest of the newspaper as if nothing happened. In a speech in 2002, Michael Crichton called this the “Gell-Mann amnesia effect”. I see this with my use of LLMs, too: I’m very critical of what they produce for coding or what they say about architectural decisions, but then when I ask them about the best grammar book to learn Romanian or how to deal with real estate agencies in Italy, I tend to easily trust them without verifying too much, making excuses for myself like “it’s just to check”, “this is common knowledge, it can’t really be off”. The problem with this is that if you are not aware of the phenomenon, you can easily get overconfident in your ability to produce good work, especially as LLMs are notoriously bad at judging some very important aspects of software development, such as maintainability or the architecture of large projects. You can make a shiny website that looks professional but is a mountain of spaghetti code under the hood, full of security holes and hidden bugs. But if you don’t have the actual competence to judge these problems, you won’t see them and will focus on the appearance, thinking that with your “friend Claude” you can do the same as more…
